In the context of machine learning and AI, zero-shot generalization typically refers to the ability of a model to perform well on a new task or concept without having to be trained on any data related to that task or concept. In other words, the model can generalize to a new task or concept without any prior knowledge or training.

In the case of text-to-image AIs, the definition of zero-shot generalization is more nuanced. Text-to-image AIs are trained on a large dataset of text-image pairs, where the text is used to generate an image. The model learns to map text to images through a complex process of feature extraction, attention mechanisms, and generation.

The concept of zero-shot generalization in text-to-image AIs is more related to the ability of the model to generate images that are not present in the training data, but are still coherent and relevant to the input text. This is often referred to as "out-of-distribution" generation.

In this sense, the definition of zero-shot generalization in the paper is more aligned with the concept of "zero-shot generation" or "out-of-distribution generation", rather than the traditional definition of zero-shot generalization in machine learning.

* A text-to-image AI is trained on a dataset of images of cats and dogs. The model learns to generate images of cats and dogs based on the text input.
* If the model is given a new text input, such as "a cat playing the piano", it may not be able to generate an image of a cat playing the piano, as this is not present in the training data.

In this example, the model is not truly "zero-shot generalizing" in the sense that it is not generating an image that is completely novel and unrelated to the training data. Instead, it is generating an image that is coherent and relevant to the input text, but still within the bounds of the training data.
